lesson.title: Kicking the Dog: Redirecting Emotion to a Safer Target
lesson.summary: Displacement redirects an emotional reaction, most often anger, away from the person or situation that caused it and onto a safer, less threatening substitute.
lesson.body:
Displacement handles a strong emotion, usually anger, by keeping the feeling fully conscious but moving where it gets aimed. The person knows perfectly well that they are angry, or hurt, or frustrated. What they cannot safely do is direct that feeling at the person who actually caused it, so the ego redirects it toward a substitute target instead.

The textbook example is sometimes called the "kick the dog" pattern. A man gets chewed out by his boss at work. He cannot yell back without risking his job, so he swallows it all day, drives home, and then snaps at his kids over something trivial, or slams a door, or is short with his partner for no clear reason. None of that anger was really about the dishes left in the sink, it was about the boss, just relocated to a target that felt safer to confront. The same pattern shows up constantly in smaller ways: a student frustrated with a difficult teacher who cannot say anything in class might come home and pick a fight with a sibling instead.

The logic here is about power and risk. The original source of the anger, a boss, a teacher, an authority figure, is too dangerous to confront directly, since doing so could bring real consequences. A spouse, a sibling, or even an inanimate object is a much lower risk outlet for the same emotional charge, so the impulse gets discharged there instead.

Displacement is easy to confuse with projection, so it is worth separating them clearly. In projection, the person denies the feeling is even theirs and assigns it to someone else instead. In displacement, the person fully owns the feeling, they just aim it at the wrong target. This distinction matters for the next chapter too: sublimation is often described as a specific, more constructive relative of displacement, one where the redirected impulse gets channeled into something valuable rather than just discharged onto whoever happens to be nearby.
